vision-of-christ:
John's first vision of the exalted Christ in this passage is an innovative blending of divine, angelic, royal, priestly & prophetic symbolism, drawing from the OT, NT, Greco-Roman culture & perhaps even from beyond the Roman Empire. Commentators have suggested John is deliberately alluding to:
  • the Colossus of Rhodes
  • the bronze statues of gods & emperors that multiplied throuout the empire during the 1st century CE.

It seems that John was portraying Jesus as the ultimate living expression of divine power & glory that would overwhelm all other pretenders.
- 'Colossus of Rhodes' in Wikipedia
vision-of-christ-colossus:
[Back]

McKnight sees a strong connection between John's vision of the exalted Christ & the still-famous 'Colossus of Rhodes', one of the 7 wonders of the ancient world.
The Colossus was a massive bronze statue of Helios (the Greek god of the Sun, typically shown with a radiant crown) erected at the mouth of the harbour of Rhodes (the largest of the Dodecanese islands, about 178 km south-east of Patmos) in ~ 304 BC. This 32m high statue took 12 years to build & was toppled by an earthquake less than 60 years later, a little more than 3 centuries before John wrote Revelation. However, it remained famous throughout the Roman era (as shown in references to it by Strabo (d. ~ AD 24) & Pliny the Elder (d. AD 79)). Its ruins by the harbour were a perpetual tourist attraction until ~ AD 654 when Arabian forces raided Rhodes & had the statue broken up & the bronze fragments (more than 900 camel loads) sold for scrap.
McKnight suggests that John is portraying Jesus (with his bronze legs & feet, & radiant face) as something like the ultimate & living 'Colossus', the true God of the Sun (& everything else) who despite the onslaughts of Rome & death itself, is still standing!
- 'Colossus of Rhodes' in Wikipedia
vision-of-christ-statues:
[Back]

By John's time, there were bronze statues of the gods & emperors (such as the Apollo of Piombino, the bronze original on which the famous Augustus of Prima Porta was based, among many others ) adorned with symbols of power in almost every city & town of the empire.
turned-voice:
This noticeably ironic statement is entirely justified in the context of Revelation: John is hearing THE Voice himself, the most direct expression of the divine heart & mind, the very Word of God (cf. Rev 19:13; see also John 1:1-3).
Given the deep roots Revelation has in Genesis, it is also significant that John here, at the end of the Biblical canon, turned towards 'the voice' (την φωνην (tēn phōnēn) ≈ 'the sound', 'the voice' ) that was speaking.' He is doing the opposite of what Adam & Eve did at the beginning of the Biblical story; when they heard 'the sound (την φωνην in the LXX) of the Lord God walking in the garden', they turned away & 'hid themselves from the Lord God' (Gen 3:8).
lampstands:
For readers of the OT, this phrase would immediately call to mind:
  • the 7 lamps of the golden branched lampstand placed in the Tabernacle (Exod 25:31-37), now commonly known as a 'menorah'
  • the 10 golden lampstands made by Solomon for the first Temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 7:48-49)
  • the golden lampstand with 7 lamps seen by Zechariah in his 5th vision (Zech 4:1-2).

Later in this chapter, the exalted Christ identifies these 7 lamps in this vision as the 7 churches themselves (1:20).
midst:
There is much that is startling in this first image of the exalted Christ, but upon reflection perhaps the most wondrous element is that Jesus (in all his glory, majesty, power & love) is 'in the midst', among the churches, up close & personal to his people. The coming messages to the 7 churches will reveal how well he knows what they are experiencing, where they are 'victorious' & where they are most at risk of compromise, both as communities & as individuals.
This resonates with God's promise to Israel & Jesus' promises in the Gospels to always be with us (Deuteronomy 31:6, Isaiah 43:2, Matt 28:20, John 14:18-23), but perhaps this vision reveals how disturbing rather than just comforting his presence may be!
son-of-man:
John's description here resonates with previous use of this title by:
  • Ezekiel,
  • Daniel&
  • Jesus.

John's use here is clearly intended to identify this exalted figure with both the Jesus of the Gospels (cf. Luke 21:25-28) & the Son of Man of Daniel's vision (cf. Dan 7:13-14).
Ezekiel:
[Back]

One of the OT books John draws on heavily in the text of Revelation is the prophet Ezekiel. In Ezekiel's visions, God consistently refers to the prophet as 'son of man' (cf. 2:1f, 3:1f, 4:1, 5:1, & so on). The title in Ezekiel seems to used to emphasise the prophet's limited & lowly humanity before the Lord God.
Daniel:
[Back]

John also draws constantly on the visions of Daniel the OT prophet in the text of Revelation, & in the apocalyptic tradition that developed in the centuries between those 2 books, any use of the phrase 'one like a son of man' is a deliberate allusion to the 'one like a son of man' in Daniel's vision of the 4 beasts.
In that vision, against the backdrop of the rise of successive beastly human kingdoms (including Rome itself as 'a fourth beast, terrible & dreadful & exceedingly strong'), this 'one like a son of man' comes as a heavenly figure before the Ancient of days to receive 'dominion & glory a&nd kingdom ... an everlasting dominion' (Dan 7:13-14). In this vision (& in the apocalyptic tradition developing in the centuries after it - cf. 1 Enoch 46) the title 'son of man' (despite its apparent emphasis on the humanity of the Person being identified) actually came to have heavenly, transcendent & even divine connotations.
The overall message of Revelation obviously resonates deeply with that vision of Daniel; indeed, John's numerous allusions to Daniel's visions (especially in chapters 7 & 10) indicate that he saw his own visions as continuous with Daniel's, & perhaps as clarifying those earlier visions.
Jesus:
[Back]

Jesus had previously (in his earthly ministry) taken the somewhat ambiguous phrase 'son of man' as perhaps his favourite self-designation. He uses it more than 80 times in total in the 4 Gospels. (cf. Matthew 9:6, 12:40, 19:28, Mark 8:38, 10:45, 13:26, John 1:51, 3:13-15, 12:23, 31-36).
It seems Jesus deliberately chose this somewhat ambiguous designation precisely because it was ambiguous! In light of Ezekiel's use, it may be understood as a self-deprecating title of humility, emphasising that Jesus shares in our humanity; Jesus' use of the term in much of his public teaching certainly allowed for this interpretation, avoiding the inevitable conflicts with Jewish authorities if he made public, overt & unambiguous claims to messianic titles.
In light of Daniel & the apocalyptic tradition, however, this self-designation may indeed be understood as a massianic claim, with Jesus identifying himself as the somewhat shadowy but clearly heavenly figure in Daniel chapter 7. In his more private teaching & conversations with the disciples, especially towards the end of his ministry, this is the meaning that emerges (cf. Luke 21:25-28).
Further, in his confrontation with the high priest in his trial (cf. Luke 22:66-71), it is very clear that Jesus is indeed making exactly that claim, & it is clearly what the high priest understood him to be saying!
robe:
The clothing of the exalted Christ here (along with other elements of John's description) resonates with the garments of:
  • a High Priest,
  • a King &
  • a Prophet.

As Barclay concludes, "When we trace the origins of the thought of John, we see that by the very dress of the Risen Lord he is showing him to us in his threefold eternal office of Prophet, Priest & King ..."
- Barclay's commentary
priest:
[Back]

The Greek word here for robe (ποδηρης ≈ 'podērēs' ≈ a long robe or tunic that reaches down to the feet) is used in the LXX (Greek translation of the OT) for the robe of the high priest (cf. Exod 28:4 in LXX; Exod 29:5 in LXX; Zech 3:4-5 in LXX).
Josephus similary describes the priestly garments worn in the 1st century by those serving in the Temple: "a long robe, reaching to his feet" & a girdle "a little above the elbows ... embroidered with flowers ..." For the High Priest, this girdle also has "a mixture of gold interwove" (Josephus: Antiquities, 3.7:2 4).
In other words, the exalted Christ is dressed very much like a High Priest (cf. Heb 4:14-16).
- Barclay's commentary
king:
[Back]

This type of robe (ποδηρης ≈ 'podērēs' ≈ a long robe or tunic that reaches down to the feet) along with the high girdle was also worn by princes & kings in Israel & other ANE nations.
In the LXX, this included the robes of Jonathan (1 Sam 18:4), Saul (1 Sam 24:4) & the 'princes of the sea' (Ezek 26:16), who were probably merchant-princes of Tyre.
To Greco-Roman eyes, Jesus' attire may well have appeared like one of the 'kings of the east' (cf. 16:12f.). The dreaded Parthian kings across the Euphrates, who had long resisted & rivalled Roman power, wore decorated long robes & tunics, & their gods were often described as 'high-girt' (eg. Yasht 15:54-57).
Hence, the risen Christ, once a lowly peasant crucified as a naked criminal, is now dressed like a king ... & a dangerous king at that!
- Barclay's commentary
prophet:
[Back]

The garments (along with other elements of the description) of the exalted Christ here are also reminiscent of the angelic messenger who visited Daniel in the third year of Cyrus (cf. Dan 10:4-6). The Biblical words for 'angel' (Hedrew מַלְאָךְ ≈ 'malʾāk' ≈ Greek ἄγγελος ≈ 'angelos') both meant 'messenger', & are used for both:
  • heavenly messengers, like the 'angels' of Christian tradition (cf. Ex 3:2 in LXX, Zech 1:11 in LXX, Matt 28:2 in NT, Acts 5:19 in NT), &
  • human messengers, like prophets or just someone carrying a message! (cf. 2 Kings 5:10 in LXX, Haggai 1:13 in LXX, Luke 7:24 in NT, James 2:25 in NT).

So the exalted Christ here appears as a 'messenger' in the same role (given he is 'a son of man') as a prophet. In fact, he is THE messenger, the Word, the ultimate expression of the heart & mind of God to his people.
- Barclay's commentary
white-wool:
This description echoes the description of the Ancient of Days, the Lord God, in Daniel's vision of the beastly kingdoms (Dan 7:9). It seems intended to represent great age (eternal existence), absolute purity (cf. Isa 1:18) & God's activity as a wise old teacher (cf. Chagidah 14).
In John's use here, this symbolises & asserts the eternal preexistence, absolute purity & wisdom of Jesus Christ.
eyes-fire:
John agains draws an image from Daniel, in his description of the angelic messenger who visited Daniel in the 3rd year of Cyrus (cf. Dan 10:6).
It seems intended to indicate omniscience (an all-perceiving gaze), righteous judgement (ability to discern truth & authority to judge) & divine majesty (highlighting the overwhelming glory, brilliance & authority of a heavenly being).
There may also be an echo here of apostolic memory. The Gospels never give a physical description of Jesus, but they often refer to the way Jesus looked at people (cf. Mt 19:26, Mk 3:5,34, Lk 22:61, Jn 1:47-48).
In John's use here, this symbolises & asserts the divinely-given authority & ability of Jesus Christ as both witness & judge.
feet-bronze:
John continues to draw on Daniel's description of the angelic messenger in chapter 10 (10:6). Ezekiel gives a similar description of angelic legs & feet in his first vision (1:4-7), & even of the lower body of the One he saw seated on the lapis lazuli throne in that vision (1:26-27).
The word used here, χαλκολίβανος ('chalkolibanos') is rare & of uncertain meaning, but is usually taken to mean a highly polished & brilliant metal. Some scholars speculate it refers to a particular metal alloy that was popular in Asia Minor, particularly Thyatira, suggesting it would have been a well-understood term in that context.
In John's use here, this seems intended to indicate strength & steadfastness, & an intense purity & glory, distinguishing heavenly messengers from human beings. It may also imply the ability to crush all enemies 'beneath his feet'. Barclay also suggests "the shining rays stand for speed, for the swiftness of the feet of God to help his own or to punish sin."
many-waters:
John earlier described 'the voice' as "loud ... like a trumpet", but here as "like the sound of many waters." Several OT passages relate the divine presence or voice to the roar of 'many waters' (eg. Ps 29:3-4), especially in the visions of Ezekiel (cf. 1:24, 43:2).
There may also be here an allusion to the roar of the Aegean Sea especially during storms that must have frequently filled little Patmos with the thunderous sound of 'many waters'!
In John's use here, it seems intended to indicate how overwhelming, unignorable & God-like was the presence & voice of the exalted Christ.
held-stars:
This image of the exalted Christ holding 'seven stars' in his right hand (representing authority) is culturally significant in numerous ways:
  • the Hebrew scriptures often speak of Yahweh's authority over the stars.
  • the Jewish NT writers allude to these OT themes.
  • this image is a rejection of the astrology that had become ubiquitous & influential throughout every level of Greco-Roman culture.
  • this image also subverted the use Domitian had made of a similar image as imperial propaganda late in the 1st century.

Overall, John is insisting that it is Jesus - the Word of God in Creation, redemption & judgement - who holds power & authority over the cosmos & the futures of men & women - not the old pagan gods, nor the newly deified gods of emperor-worship!
Later in the context of this passage, Jesus will identify the 7 stars for John as the 7 angels of the churches.
Note - comments regarding the identity of these 'stars'/angels are attached to those words of Jesus (v.20).
jewish-stars:
[Back]

In the OT, there are many affirmations that the Lord God is the who created & directs the stars (eg. Gen 1:16, Ps 8:3-4, 33:6 & 147:4; Isa 40:26 & 45:12).
In response, the stars along with all Creation were regarded as declaring the glory of God (eg. Ps 19:1), & as symbols both of God's promises to his people (eg. Gen 15:5) & of the illuminating influence of his righteous people in the world (eg. Dan 12:3).
nt-stars:
[Back]

The NT writers echo several of the OT themes regarding stars (eg. Heb 11:12, Philippians 2:14-16, Eph 5:8-10, 2 Cor 4:6).
astrology:
[Back]

Greco-Roman astrology (based on the more ancient Babylonian/Chaldean, Assyrian, Persian, Greek & Roman cultures) identified 'the seven stars' as the 7 astronomical bodies which move against the background of the 'fixed' stars of the constellations; that is, the Sun, the Moon & the 5 planets visible to the naked eye, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter & Saturn.
From the beginning, these seven 'stars' were associated with certain gods, & the movement of these 'stars' was believed to influence the lives of individuals & communities on Earth.
By the NT era, the Romans had renamed these 'stars' with the names of their own divinities. One expression of this was the 'planetary week' that had come into use by Romans in the NT era.
This all reflected & reinforced the belief that these 7 'lords of time' (χρονοκράτορες ≈ 'chronokratores'), these 7 wandering 'stars', have power & control over hours & days, & furthermore, power to influence earthly affairs & the lives & fates of human beings.
In the context of the Greco-Roman culture of these 7 cities (and of the empire as a whole), John's picture here subverts the assumptions of the old religions & astrology, asserting that it is the exalted Christ who holds 'the seven stars' in his right hand (symbolising power & authority). He is the true & ultimate 'time-lord' with a sovereign influence over the cosmos, & over the circumstances of individuals, communities & indeed, the world.
Bultrighini:
[Back]

As Bultrighini observes, "Astrology was not only a system of divination claiming to predict the future by observing the stars: it implied a religious conception of the world, its starting point being the faith in celestial divinities that were thought to exert an influence on the world."
By Greco-Roman times,'Chaldaean wisdom' was a synonym for astrology (divination through the planets & stars). Astrologers became very much in vogue in Imperial Rome.
associated:
[Back]

Keep in mind the planets were not merely named after gods & goddesses of the Graeco-Roman pantheon but became very closely identified with those deities in the cultural & religious imagination of the 1st century empire as manifestations or vehicles of the gods' power.
planets:
[Back]

The Greek word for these 'stars' that moved against the backdrop of the fixed stars (πλανῆται ≈ 'planētai' ≈ 'wanderers') is the basis for our English word for 'planets'. Keep in mind, though, the ancient cultures included the Sun & the Moon with these wandering 'stars'.
divinities:
[Back]

The Greek & Roman gods identified with the 7 'stars' were:
  • Kronos > Saturnus - Saturn
  • Helios > Sol - Sun
  • Selene > Luna - Moon
  • Ares > Mars - Mars
  • Hermes > Mercurius - Mercury
  • Zeus > Iupiter - Jupiter
  • Aphrodite > Venus - Venus
planetary-week:
[Back]

The 'planetary week' identified each day of the week with one of the divine 'wanderers', the 'seven stars', as follows:
  • Saturn > Saturday
  • Sun > Sunday
  • Moon > Monday
  • Mars > Tuesday
  • Mercury > Wednesday
  • Jupiter > Thursday
  • Venus > Friday
Domitian:
[Back]

Domitian became emperor in AD 81, & his only son & heir died less than 2 years later (a decade or so before Revelation was written). This effectively ended the direct Flavian line of succession - the 'dynastic security' that was a central part of their propaganda - & it was something of a crisis for the imperial ideology.
Domitian attempted to salvage the situation by having his deceased son deified, then minting coins to show his son as Divus Caesar ('Divine Caesar') very soon after the boy died. While this officially elevated the status of the Flavian family to a semi-divine level, it also served as a constant public reminder of the emperor's failure to provide a living heir.
Signifantly, the obverse of the coins, which were in circulation through-out the empire for a decade before John's vision on Patmos, showed the boy seated upon a globe (representing the universe/cosmos, not the earth), reaching out towards 7 stars. This portrayed him as something of a 'young Jupiter' who continues to rule the universe (directing the stars) from the heavens.
Hence John's portrait of Jesus in Revelation 1 subverts the imperial ideology, asserting that it is Christ (revealed by John's vision in divine glory) who holds & exerts ultimate power over both heaven & earth, not the emperors, whether living or dead-&-deified!
imperial-ideology:
[Back]

In imperial ideology, the emperor was deified after death when the Senate voted a decree of apotheosis (deification), making him a divus ('divine one') & thus officially a god of the Roman state. Worship of a living emperor - such as demanded by Domitian requiring subjects to address him as dominus et deus ('Lord & God') - was framed as veneration of the genius (divine nature) of the emperor or of the Roman state itself.
Full deification was reserved for the post-mortem ritual of apotheosis. That was alao when the emporer's son & heir would recieve the title of Divi filius ('son of a god' or 'son of the divine').
sword:
This unusual image of a long sword coming from the mouth of Jesus is startling visually, but also linguistically - the 'sword' here is an uncommon ῥομφαία ('rhomphaia') ... especially as it is 'two-edged'!
This image (& word) is significant in light of the OT (especially the LXX from ~250 BC), the NT & the Roman imperial context.
John's repeated use of 'rhomphaia' in Revelation as a clear metaphor for the 'Word' of Christ almost certainly relates to:
  • the formidable power of this weapon;
  • its frequent use in the LXX in apocalyptic &/or eschatological passages regarding the judgement & saving actions of God on behalf of "the faithful ... the humble' whom 'he adorns with victory' (Psalm 149);
  • its historical use as a weapon of resistance against the empire.
rhomphaia:
[Back]

Ῥομφαία ('rhomphaia') in ancient Greek texts has traditionally been translated into English as 'battle axe' or 'broadsword', but this class of weapons were more like modified spears with a long heavy iron single-edged blade (either straight or slightly curved towards the sharp edge) up to 80cm long & a wooden handle up to about 50cm long. Rhomphaias were first designed & used in Thrace as early as the 4th century BC.
Longer versions were wielded with 2 hands, giving the weapon great reach (well beyond the range of a Roman soldier's 60-85cm gladius) & immense striking power. This is reflected in the Latin forms of the word which include rumpia, romphea & romphaea vel romfea, all related to the Latin verb rumpo, meaning 'to break' or 'to destroy'.
'Rhomphaia' may also be etymologically related to the words for 'thunderbolt' or 'lightning' in Bulgaria (which overlaps with ancient Thrace) - roféja, rufja - & nearby Albania - rrufeja.
two-edged:
[Back]

Historically, Ῥομφαία ('rhomphaia') all had single-edged blades. Some centuries after John, authors did begin describing large two-edged swords as rhomphaias, but not in the 1st century.
John's innovation here of a double-edged rhomphaia may be:
  • a magnification of the formidable power of an already fearsome weapon;
  • an echo of the unique eschatological 'two-edged' rhomphaia used by 'the faithful' in Psalm 149 in the LXX to execute God's judgement on the nations;
  • related to the dual role of the Word of God in His dealing with humanity, both to judge & to save - the early church fathers had this in mind when they identified the 2 edges as the Law & the Gospel (cf. Victorinus (~ AD 300), Expositio Apocalypsis);
  • the direction of that 'sword' towards the church first (in disciplining the churches in ch.2-3) & then towards the nations (in judgement towards individuals, nations & even fallen angels).
sword-OT:
[Back]

The OT frequently depicts God (or his angel/s or his people) wielding or commanding a sword as an instrument of judgment, warfare, divine justice or even protection (cf. Genesis 3:24 - 1st occurrence of 'sword', Isaiah 27:1 - a classic divine-combat image, Isaiah 27:1 - the Lord's sword in final judgement).
There are also some passages that make it clear it is actually the Word (or words) of God that are the ultimate 'weapon' of judgement, revelation & redemption (cf. Isaiah 49:2, Hosea 6:5, Jeremiah 23:29).
rhomphaia-LXX:
[Back]

Ῥομφαία ('rhomphaia') was used by the LXX translators about 200 times in the OT to translate חֶרֶב ('chereb'), a generic Hebrew word for 'sword'. They also used μάχαιρα ('machaira') about 170 times as well, denoting a short sword or large knife for routine use.
Ezekiel (a book John draws on heavily) is notable as 'rhomphaia' appears more then 40 times. This sword is frequently directed in judgement against Judah &/or Israel (eg. 21:3-27), & at times against others (eg. 21:28-32 - against Ammon, 30:1-26 - against Egypt).
Ezekiel actually referred to Babylon's forces as the 'rhomphaia' of Yahweh. It would be other prophets like Isaiah (ch. 13-14) & Jeremiah (ch. 50-51) who would prophecy against Babylon itself. It seems Ezekiel, while exiled in Babylon, views Babylon as a temporary instrument in God's plan, rather than an existential enemy of God's people.
Historically, rhomphaias were not developed until around the end of the OT period (~ 400 BC) but it appears the LXX translators (~ 250 BC) preferred to use the more vivid & formidable 'rhomphaia' in prophetic & apocalyptic declarations of God's overwhleming judgment, evoking for their readers a heightened sense of decisive violence or even terrifying, divine-scale destruction. This is true even in Psalm 149:6, describing 'the faithful' enacting God's judgement on the nations using 'two-edged rhomphaias' to 'wreak vengance ... & chastisement' ... even though rhomphaias only had a single edge!
sword-empire:
[Back]

The image of Jesus with this imposing sword emerging from his mouth challenged the imperial Roman ideology in several ways:
  • it subverted the implicit claim of military, judicial & even divine authority asserted in iconography showing emperors & Roman deities adorned with daggers & swords (especially the gladius & the decorative parazonium), deliberately reinforced &/or utilised by several emperors in the second half of the 1st century;
  • it asserted Jesus is the One with the ultimate 'right of the sword';
  • the 'rhomphaia' had historical connotations of resistance against the empire.
emperors-deities-sword:
[Back]

Some specific examples are:
  • Roman gods, including:
    • Mars
    • Roma
  • Roman emperors, including:
    • Augustus, in both:
      • Augustus Prima Porta
      • The Gemma Augustea
    • Trajan
ius-gladii:
[Back]

In the Roman Empire, the sword was a symbol of the highest order of official authority, whether poitical, military or judicial. All 3 dimensions of authority are enshrined in the Roman legal concept of ius gladii ('jus gladii') which is usually translated as the 'right of the sword'.
Originally used in military discipline as the power to execute soldiers, during the 1st century it became more broadly applied as the right to execute Roman citizens, usually in judicial proceedings. By John's time, this right rested primarily with the emperor as a core symbol of imperial power, & he bequeathed it to provincial governors (by virtue of their office for Senatorial governors - as in Asia Minor - or by decree for selected Equestrian governors, such as Pontius Pilate in Judea).
John's portrayal of Jesus is an overt claim that the true & ultimate ius gladii, the power of life & death, rests not with the Roman emperor or his governors, but with the exalted & soon-to-return Christ who's words are the irresistible instruments of judgement, justice & salvation.
- Ramsay on ius gladii
sword-emperors:
[Back]

The symbolic significance of the sword for the emperor's position in the empire is evident from the principle of ius gladii, but also from the use of that symbol made by several emperors, including:
  • Galba (reigned 7 months, June AD 68 to January 69) - hearing of Nero's death, he donned a in a general's cloak & marched to Rome with a dagger hanging from his neck to claim the throne (cf. Suetonius, Life of Galba;
  • Vitellius (reigned 8 months, April to December 69) - after his forces lost in a crushing defeat to rebel forces seeking to put Vespasian (governor of Judea) on the throne, he attempted to abdicate to avoid more bloodshed & to save his family. He symbolised this by offering his pugio ('dagger') to a consul in an assembly, giving up this 'imperial insignia' "as if surrendering his power of life & death over the citizens' (cf. Tacitus, Histories, III, 68.)
  • Trajan (reigned 19½ years, January AD 98 to August 117) - when he assumed the throne, Trajan famously presented a large sword to the newly appointed prefect of the Praetorian Guard, pronouncing "Take this sword, in order that, if I rule well, you may use it for me, but if ill, against me." The sword symbolised the supreme executive & judicial power of the office, as well as Trajan's accountability to the military (cf. Cassius Dio, Historiae Romanae, 68:16 & Pliny, Panegyricus Traiani, 67.)
rhomphaia-empire:
[Back]

The rhomphaia was a formidable & feared weapon in the ancient Roman imagination.
Developed by early in the 4th century BC, it gained infamy when used by Thracian mercenaries fighting for King Perseus against Romans forces in the Third Macedonian War in the 2nd century BC. Accounts from those present describe the advance of Thracians armed with their 'rhomphaias' as "most terrible".
By late in the 1st century AD, the Dacians from northern Thrace had developed a modified rhomphaia with a more curved sickle-like blade which the Romans called a falx ('sickle'). Displayed on Trajan's Column, erected in the centre of Rome to commemorate Trajan's eventual victory over the Dacians, these weapons were symbols of resistance against the Roman Empire.
falx:
[Back]

The falx were used against Roman soldiers first in Domitian's Dacian War in the decade before John wrote Revelation, then in Trajan's Dacian Wars in the decade after.
The falx was a devastating weapon in the hands of a trained warrior. Its length, sharp point & curved blade made it capable of striking with great force, with the point piercing helmets, the blade splitting shields (completely in a single blow, it was said) or used as a hook to pull away shields or amputate vulnerable limbs.
During Domitian's war, Roman military engineers made the only recorded adjustments to their helmets & armour prompted by encounters with a new enemy weapon. They reinforced helmets with metal bands & arm guards & greaves protecting the lower legs became more common. Trajan would go further, adjusting battle tactics to neutralise the advantages of the falx.
Plutarch:
[Back]

Plutarch, writing his Parallel Lives a decade or 2 after John wrote Revelation, gave an account of the battle of Pydna in the Third Macedonian War (~168 BC). He recounts descriptions given by eyewitnesses of the appearance 'most terrible' of the Thracian warriors & their fearsome 'heavy-ironed rhomphaias'.
Dacians:
[Back]

Dacians came from an area near the Carpathian Mountains west of the Black Sea at the northern end of Thrace & are often considered a subgroup of the Thracians. They are first mentioned by Herodotus in his Histories (~ late 5th century BC), where he describes them as "the noblest as well as the most just of all the Thracian tribes."
rhomphaia-NT:
[Back]

Both Paul the Apostle (Eph 6:17) & the author of Hebrews (4:12) had previously used imagery identifying the Word of God as a sword ('machaira'), highlighting its role as both a defensive spiritual 'weapon' & a penetrating force.
However, John's use of 'rhomphaia' here & elsewhere in Revelation is distinctive.
distinctive:
[Back]

'Sword' appears 36 times in the English NT, with 29 of those instances using the word μάχαιρα ('machaira', as used in Ephesians & Hebrews), a broad Hellenistic Greek term for any large knife, short sword or curved/large slashing blade.
There are, indeed, 2 occurences of 'machaira' in Revelation (cf. 6:4, 13:10) in apparent references to human violence. The word ῥομφαία ('rhomphaia'), however, occurs only once outside Revelation, as a metaphor in Luke 2:35.
In contrast, 'rhomphaia' occurs 6 times in Revelation (here in 1:16, then in 2:12, 2:16, 6:8, 19:15 & 19:21). All but 1 instance refer to the sword coming from the mouth of the exalted Christ; the sole exception is the sword used by 'Death & Hades' in 6:8.
face-sun:
This image has resonances with:
  • passages elsewhere in Revelation
  • passages in other NT books
  • passages in the OT
  • sections in other Jewish apocalyptic literature
  • imagery in Greco-Roman culture
face-sun-rev:
[Back]

This image resonates with other passages in Revelation, including:
  • 4:2-6 ... John describes the 'one seated on the throne' & his throne-room with symbolic references to the brilliance, light & colour of precious gemstones, 'a rainbow that looked like an emerald', 'flashes of lightning' & 'a sea of glass like crystal.'
  • 10:1 ... John describes a 'mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, & his face was like the sun, & his legs like pillars of fire', echoing descriptions of both the exalted Christ (in ch.1) & the enthroned Lord God (in ch.4).
  • 21:11 ... John describes the New Jerusalem 'coming down out of heaven from God' illuminated by 'the glory of God, its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal.'
  • 21:23-25 ... John continues his description of the New Jerusalem, insisting that 'the city has no need of sun or moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God is its light, & its lamp is the Lamb ... there shall be no night there.' This portrayal of God (& with him, Jesus the Lamb) as the eternal light of His redeemed people (reiterated once more in 22:5) echoes the promise in Isaiah 60:19-20.
face-sun-NT:
[Back]

This image resonates with passages from each section of the NT, including:
  • the Gospels
  • the Acts
  • the Letters

Overall, these NT parallels indicate John is portraying Jesus with the overwhelming radiance of transcendent divine presence, & hence his presence 'in the midst' of the seven ekklesias makes them part of the sacred space of the heavenly temple of which he is the ultimate High Priest.
face-sun-gospels:
[Back]

The Gospels frequently use 'light' as a central metaphor for the identity & mission of Jesus, including in:
  • Matthew 17:2 ... the 'Transfiguration', when Jesus & 3 of his disciples (including John!) went up 'a high mountain apart' & 'he was transfigured before them, & his face shone like the sun, & his garments became white as light', then 'a bright cloud overshadowed them' & God spoke to them from the cloud (cf. Luke 9:28-35).
  • Luke 1:76-79 ... Zechariah's prophecy over his baby son implies that Jesus' coming will be 'when the day shall dawn upon us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness & in the shadow of death.'
  • Luke 2:29-32 ... in old Simeon's prayer over the baby Jesus, he called him 'thy salvation ... a light for revelation to the nations.'
  • John 1:1-9, 8:12, 9:5 ... the 4th Gospel begins by potraying Jesus in sun-like terms as 'the light of men' that 'shines in the darkness ... the true light that enlightens every man'. Later, Jesus announced in the temple in Jerusalem that 'I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life' & 'as long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.'

Perhaps the more startling passages are those that imply that his disciples are called to somehow play a part in bringing this divine 'light of the world' to other individuals, communities & even the world! Some examples are in:
  • Matthew 5:14-16... Jesus tells his disciples 'you are the light of world ... Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works & give glory to your Father who is in heaven.'
  • John 12:35-36... John the Baptist s described as the very first 'to bear witness to the light, that all might believe through him.'
  • John 12:35-36... Jesus instructs his disciples to 'believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.'
face-sun-acts:
[Back]

This image resonates with some passages from Acts (the sequel to Luke's Gospel), including:
  • Acts 2:1-4 ... when the Holy Spirit descended on the embryonic church with 'a sound ... like the rush of a mighty wind' & 'appeared to them tongues as of fire, distributed & resting on each one of them.' These signs of divine presence implied that the Christian ekklesia was now the 'sacred place', the temple in which the presence of Yahweh dwelt;
  • Acts 26:12f ... Saul of Tarsus saw 'a light from heaven, brighter than the sun' & heard the voice (φωνην ≈ 'phōnēn') of 'Jesus whom you are persecuting' give him a commission to the Gentiles (the 'nations'), 'to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light.'

Both of these passages imply that the Christian community across the empire is indwelt by the divine presence of the Holy Spirit & are now conduits for God's illuminating life & message: they are to be indeed 'the light of the world'!
face-sun-letters:
[Back]

The NT Letters repeatedly echo & expand on the imagery from the Gospels, relating light metaphorically to:
  • the essential nature of God
  • the identity & glory of Jesus
  • & the spiritual identity of his followers
face-sun-letters-God:
[Back]

The apostles oftem use light to represent God's absolute holiness, purity, & unapproachable glory. Examples include:
  • James 1:17 ... in perhaps the first of the NT letters, Jesus' little brother uses the very Hebrew description of God as 'the Father of lights with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.'
  • 1 Timothy 6:13-16 ... in this almost startling charge to his younger apprentice, the Apostle Paul refers to God as 'the blessed & only Sovereign, the King of kings & Lord of lords, who alone has immortality & dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man has ever seen or can see.'
  • 1 John 1:5-7 ... in his first letter that shares numerous themes with both the 4th Gospel & Revelation, John asserts that 'God is light & in him is no darkness at all ... if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, & the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin'
face-sun-letters-Jesus:
[Back]

Several apostolic writers identify Jesus with 'light' through descriptions of his divine glory, the 'light of the gospel,' & his role as the source of enlightenment for believers, including:
  • Paul the Apostle in several letters
  • the unknown author of Hebrews, who insisted that 'the Son is the radiance of God's glory & the exact representation of his being' (1:3).
  • Peter the Apostle who affirmed that Christians in the midst of the paga Roman Empire were 'a royal priesthood, a holy nation' called by God 'out of darkness into his wonderful light.'
  • & John the Apostle, who indicates that 'if we walk in the light, as he is in the light', it is because 'the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin' (1 John 1:7).
face-sun-letters-Jesus-Paul:
[Back]

Relevant passages include:
  • 2 Corinthians 3:17-4:6 ... Paul asserts that those with the Spirit of the Lord experience 'freedom & ... are being changed into his likeness from one degree of glory to another.' He insists it is unbelievers' minds which are veiled 'to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the likeness of God,' & 'it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.
  • Colossians 1:12-15 ... in his prayer & thankgiving, Paul refers to 'the inheritance of the saints in light' given that God 'has delivered us from the dominion of darkness & transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son' who 'is the image of the invisible God, the first-born of all creation.'
face-sun-letters-followers:
[Back]

Christians are frequently identified as 'light' due to their new identity in Christ, the transformation of their behaviour & lifestyles, & their witness to Jesus. Relevant passages include:
  • Paul the Apostle in several letters
  • Peter the Apostle, who insists that since God has called Jesus-followers 'out of darkness into his wonderful light,' they should now 'abstain from sinful desires, which wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds & glorify God on the day he visits us'(1 Peter 2:9-12).
  • John the Apostle asserts in his 1st letter that 'God is light' & 'if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another' & with Him (1:6-7). Hence, since 'the darkness is passing away & the true light is already shining', loving others is the clearest indication that one 'abides in the light' (2:8-11).
face-sun-letters-followers-Paul:
[Back]

Relevant passages include:
  • 1 Thessalonians 5:4-8 ... Paul reminds the Thessalonians 'you are not in darkness ... you are all sons of light & sons of the day.' Therefore, 'let us be sober, & put on the breastplate of faith & love, & for a helmet the hope of salvation.'
  • 2 Corinthians 4:6 ... Paul tells the Corinthians that God has 'shone in our hearts' so that believers (including apostles) may reflect and 'give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ'
  • Romans 13:11-14 ... Paul urges the Romans to 'cast off the works of darkness & put on the armor of light' which means to 'make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.'
  • Philippians 2:15 ... Paul reminds teh Philippians that if they live as 'blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish,' they will 'shine as lights in the world.'
  • Ephesians 5:8-14 ... Paul makes the startling assertion to Christians that 'now you are light in the Lord' so you should 'walk as children of light.' He suggests that 'when anything is exposed by the light it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light.'. He then quotes from what is probably an early Christian hymn (probably alluding to Isaiah 60:1) used in baptisms or other liturgies:
    Awake, O sleeper, & arise from the dead, & Christ shall give you light.
face-sun-OT:
[Back]

John's image of Jesus' face shining like the sun relates to numerous OT passages from some very significant eras or moments in the history of Israel as God's people, including :
  • in the exodus from Egypt.
  • in the formative era of the Judges
  • at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem
  • during the divided kingdom
  • during & after the exile to Babylon

Overall, the OT suggests that overwhelming radiance (such as a 'face ... like the sun shining in full strength') indicates the divine presence, either directly or reflected by a heavenly messenger or 'friend of God.' All these apply to Jesus, the divine Son who is 'one with the Father' (cf. John 10:30-38) & whose presence suggests the 7 Christian ekklesia (symbolising all Christian churches) are 'sacred space', the Temple of God & Christ.
face-sun-exodus:
[Back]

Relevant passages from the period of the Exodus include:
  • Exodus 3:1-6 ... The 'angel of the Lord' (later just 'the Lord') appeared to Moses as 'in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush', & yet 'the bush ... was not consumed'. As Moses came close, 'God called to him out of the bush ... "Do not come near; put off your shoes from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."' The radiant presence of Yahweh made this place a temple, a 'sacred space'.
  • Exodus 40:34-38 ... the radiant presence of God was experienced by Israel as a pillar of fire in the wilderness & as an overwhelming cloud of 'glory' & 'fire' filling the Tabernacle.
  • Exodus 34:29-35 ... when Moses met with God on Mt Sinai, his face would shine so that people were fearful of approach him.
  • Numbers 6:23-26 ... the priestly blessing over Israel includes the exhortation that 'the Lord make his face shine on you.' This prayer is later echoed in several psalms (eg. Ps 80:3,7,19) & in Daniel's prayer for Jerusalem (Dan 9:17).
face-sun-judges:
[Back]

A relevant passages from the period of Judges is Judges 5:31. Deborah & Barak's song (after defeating the Canaanites who had oppressed Israel for 20 years & the humiliating death of the Canaanite commander) ends with the line (perhaps inspired by memories of Moses, the friend of God - cf. Exod 33:11): 'So perish all thine enemies, O Lord! But thy friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.'
face-sun-temple:
[Back]

1 Kings 8:10-11 records that when Solomon dedicated the Temple in Jerusalem, an overwhelming 'cloud ... the glory of Lord filled the house of the Lord.'
2 Chronicles 7:1-3 adds that 'fire came down from heaven & consumed the burnt offering & the sacrifices ... all the children of Israel saw the fire come down & the glory of the Lord upon the temple.'
face-sun-divided:
[Back]

Isaiah, one of the greatest prophets of Israel & of the OT, uses the motif of divine light extensively to symbolise God's holiness, the coming Messiah, & the restoration of His people. For example:
  • 2:5 ... calls for the house of Jacob to 'walk in the light of the Lord.'
  • 9:2 ... prophecies that 'a great light' will dawn on 'those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness.'
  • 10:17 ... describes the Lord as a fire & light that will consume His enemies.
  • 30:26 ... promises that the moon will shine like the sun & the sun will be seven times brighter on the day the Lord heals His people.
  • 42:6 ... commissions the Servant (Messiah) to be 'a light to the nations'.
  • 49:6 ... reiterates the Messiah's role as 'a light to the nations' to bring God's salvation 'to the end of the earth'.
  • 60:1-5 ... commands Israel as God's people to 'arise, shine; for your light has come ... his glory will be seen upon you ... nations shall come to your light ... you shall see & be radiant'.
  • 60:19-20 ... promises that God will replace the sun & moon as 'your everlasting light, & your God will be your glory'.
face-sun-exile:
[Back]

Relevant passages from exilic & post-exilic prophets include:
  • Ezekiel 1:26-28 ... Ezekiel described the overwhelming appearance of the Lord in his first vision as 'like sapphire ... gleaming bronze ... the appearance of fire ... brightness round about ... the glory of the Lord.' He indicates this figure had 'a likeness ... of a human form' but (perhaps in reverence) refrained from describing the face of the Lord, even though he had earlier described in detail the faces (4 each!) of the four strange 'living creatures' that carried the throne.
  • Daniel 10:5-6 ... in his description of the heavenly messenger who came in response to his 3-week prayer vigil, Daniel says 'His body was like beryl [shining/brilliant], his face like ... lightning, his eyes like flaming torches.'
  • Daniel 9:17 ... Daniel echoes Aaron's priestly blessing on Israel, asking God to 'cause thy face to shine upon thy sanctuary, which is desolate' (Numbers 6:23-26).
  • Malachi 4:1-2 ... the last OT prophet looks forward to 'the great & terrible day of the Lord' (v.5) which fills John's visions in Revelation, when 'the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings.'
face-sun-JAL:
[Back]

This image has resonances in:
  • the OT:
    • Judges 5:31 ... the song of Deborah & Barak (after the defeat of the Canaanites who had oppressed Israel for 20 years, including the humiliating death of the commander of the Canaanite army, Sisera) finishes with the line: 'So perish all thine enemies, O Lord! But thy friends be like the sun as he rises in his might' (Judges 5:32).
    • its frequent use in the LXX in apocalyptic &/or eschatological passages regarding the judgement & saving actions of God on behalf of "the faithful ... the humble' whom 'he adorns with victory' (Psalm 149);
    • its historical use as a weapon of resistance against the empire.
